subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Structure 1.4–1.5 — counting particles by mass; ideal gases
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: The mole as a count of named particles
Relative atomic and formula mass on the carbon-12 scale
Molar mass and the n = m/M relationship
Empirical and molecular formulae from composition
Molar concentration, n = CV and unit conversions
Avogadro's law and reacting gas volumes
The assumptions of the ideal gas model
Where real gases depart from the model, and why
Molar volume and the relationships between p, V and T
Using PV = nRT and the combined gas law

questions.q: Which statement about one mole of a substance is correct?
options: It contains 6.02 × 10²³ of whichever entity is specified.
It has a mass of 12 g, whichever substance it may be.
It contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, whatever the substance.
It occupies 22.7 dm³ at 273.15 K and 100 kPa, whatever its state.
optionWhy: One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities, and the entity must be named: 1 mol of H₂O is 6.02 × 10²³ molecules but 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.

A student who thinks of the mole as a mass picks this. 12 g is the mass of one mole of carbon-12 atoms only; the mass of one mole is the molar mass, which differs between substances (18.02 g for H₂O, 58.44 g for NaCl).
A student who attaches the Avogadro constant to atoms picks this. One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ of the specified entity; 1 mol of CH₄ molecules contains 5 × 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.

A student who applies the gas molar volume to every substance picks this. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ holds only for gases (behaving ideally) at 273.15 K and 100 kPa; one mole of liquid water occupies about 18 cm³.
questions.explain: One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities, and the entity must be named: 1 mol of H₂O is 6.02 × 10²³ molecules but 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.

questions.q: How many atoms are there in 0.500 mol of water, H₂O? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
optionWhy: A student who stops at n × N_A counts molecules: 0.500 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ H₂O molecules. The question asks for atoms, and each molecule contains 3, giving 9.03 × 10²³.
Each H₂O molecule has 3 atoms. Atoms = 0.500 mol × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 9.03 × 10²³.

A student who applies the ratio of 3 atoms per molecule the wrong way round divides by 3: 3.01 × 10²³ ÷ 3 = 1.00 × 10²³. There are more atoms than molecules, so multiply: 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.

A student who counts only the atoms with a written subscript takes each H₂O molecule to have 2 atoms: 0.500 × 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²³. The O has an unwritten subscript of 1, so each molecule has 3 atoms: 0.500 × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.
questions.explain: Each H₂O molecule has 3 atoms. Atoms = 0.500 mol × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 9.03 × 10²³.
questions.working: N(molecules) = n × N_A = 0.500 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³. Each H₂O molecule contains 2 H + 1 O = 3 atoms, so N(atoms) = 3 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²³.

questions.q: A student writes: 'M_r of carbon dioxide, CO₂ = 44.01 g mol⁻¹'. Which comment on this statement is correct?
options: It is correct: M_r and molar mass are one and the same quantity.
The unit is wrong: M_r is the mass of one molecule in grams.
The unit is wrong: M_r is measured in atomic mass units.
The unit is wrong: M_r is a ratio of masses, with no unit.
optionWhy: A student who treats M_r and molar mass as one quantity accepts the unit. They share the number 44.01, but M_r is a pure number and only the molar mass M has the unit g mol⁻¹.
A student who thinks M_r is the mass of one molecule in grams picks this. 44.01 g is the mass of a mole of CO₂ molecules; one molecule has a mass of 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g. M_r itself has no unit.
A student taught that relative masses are 'in atomic mass units' picks this. The mass of one CO₂ molecule is 44.01 u, but M_r is that mass divided by the atomic mass unit, so it has no unit.
M_r compares the mass of a CO₂ molecule with one twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom, so the units cancel: M_r(CO₂) = 44.01. The quantity with unit g mol⁻¹ is the molar mass, M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: M_r compares the mass of a CO₂ molecule with one twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom, so the units cancel: M_r(CO₂) = 44.01. The quantity with unit g mol⁻¹ is the molar mass, M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹.

questions.q: The mass of one molecule of compound Z is 3.666 times the mass of one atom of carbon-12. What is the relative molecular mass, M_r, of Z?
optionWhy: A student who compares Z with a whole ¹²C atom treats the ratio as the relative mass. On the scale, a ¹²C atom is 12, not 1, so M_r = 3.666 × 12 = 43.99.
Relative masses are measured against one twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom, on which scale ¹²C = 12 exactly. M_r(Z) = 3.666 × 12 = 43.99.

A student who takes the reference to be natural carbon uses 12.01: 3.666 × 12.01 = 44.03. The stem compares Z with carbon-12, which is assigned exactly 12; 12.01 is the A_r of natural carbon, which contains some carbon-13.
A student who applies the ratio upside down calculates 12 ÷ 3.666 = 3.273. Z is heavier than a ¹²C atom, so its relative mass must be larger than 12: 3.666 × 12 = 43.99.
questions.explain: Relative masses are measured against one twelfth of the mass of a ¹²C atom, on which scale ¹²C = 12 exactly. M_r(Z) = 3.666 × 12 = 43.99.
questions.working: On the relative mass scale one ¹²C atom = 12 exactly. M_r(Z) = (mass of Z molecule ÷ mass of ¹²C atom) × 12 = 3.666 × 12 = 43.992 ≈ 43.99.

questions.q: The relative molecular mass of methane, CH₄, is 16.05. Which statement about the molar mass, M, of methane is correct?
options: It is 16.05 g; one molecule of CH₄ has a mass of 16.05 g.
It is 16.05, with no unit, as molar mass is the same as M_r.
It is 16.05 g mol⁻¹; 1 mol of CH₄ molecules has mass 16.05 g.
It is 16.05 g mol⁻¹; 16.05 g of CH₄ contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
optionWhy: A student who thinks relative or molar mass is the mass of a single molecule picks this. One CH₄ molecule has a mass of 16.05 g ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.67 × 10⁻²³ g; 16.05 g is a mole of molecules.
A student who treats molar mass and M_r as one quantity transfers 'no unit' to M. M_r has no unit, but molar mass is a mass per mole with unit g mol⁻¹.
Molar mass is mass per mole, in g mol⁻¹, and has the same number as M_r: 16.05 g is the mass of 1 mol (6.02 × 10²³) of CH₄ molecules, so M = 16.05 g mol⁻¹.
A student who thinks a mole is always 6.02 × 10²³ atoms picks this. 16.05 g of methane contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, and each has 5 atoms, so it contains 3.01 × 10²⁴ atoms.
questions.explain: Molar mass is mass per mole, in g mol⁻¹, and has the same number as M_r: 16.05 g is the mass of 1 mol (6.02 × 10²³) of CH₄ molecules, so M = 16.05 g mol⁻¹.

questions.q: What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄? (A_r: H 1.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, S 32.07)
optionWhy: A student who applies the 2 after the bracket only to the H atoms reads the formula as NH₈SO₄: M_r = 118.16 and % N = 14.01 ÷ 118.16 × 100 = 11.86%. The 2 multiplies the whole NH₄ group, giving 2 N atoms and M_r = 132.17.
A student who treats the share of atoms as the share of mass counts 2 N atoms out of 15 atoms: 2 ÷ 15 × 100 = 13.33%. Each atom must be weighted by its A_r: 28.02 ÷ 132.17 × 100 = 21.20%.

A student who divides the mass of nitrogen by the mass of the other elements calculates 28.02 ÷ (132.17 − 28.02) × 100 = 26.90%. A percentage by mass is a part of the whole: 28.02 ÷ 132.17 × 100 = 21.20%.

questions.q: The empirical formula of ethanoic acid is CH₂O. What does this empirical formula tell you about ethanoic acid?
options: Its atoms of C, H and O are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
Each of its molecules has one C atom, two H atoms and one O atom.
The masses of its C, H and O are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
Each of its C atoms is bonded to two H atoms and to one O atom.
optionWhy: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms: C₂H₄O₂ simplifies to 1 : 2 : 1, written CH₂O.
A student who takes the empirical formula to be the molecular formula picks this. Each molecule of ethanoic acid contains 2 C, 4 H and 2 O atoms; CH₂O gives only their ratio.
A student who equates the ratio of atoms with the ratio of masses picks this. The atoms have different masses: the mass ratio C : H : O is 12.01 : 2.02 : 16.00, not 1 : 2 : 1.

A student who reads a formula as a map of bonding picks this. In CH₃COOH one carbon atom carries three H atoms and no O atom, and the other carries two O atoms and no H atom. Formulae give numbers of atoms, not which are joined.
questions.explain: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms: C₂H₄O₂ simplifies to 1 : 2 : 1, written CH₂O.

questions.q: What amount of sodium hydroxide is present in 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq) in which [NaOH] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³?
options: 2.50 mol
optionWhy: A student who takes 1 dm³ as 100 cm³ converts 25.0 cm³ to 0.250 dm³: 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol. 1 dm³ = (10 cm)³ = 1000 cm³, so 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³ and n = 0.00250 mol.
A student who uses n = V/C calculates 0.0250 ÷ 0.100 = 0.250 mol. Concentration is amount per dm³, so n = C × V = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol.
A student who substitutes the volume in cm³ calculates 0.100 × 25.0 = 2.50 mol. The concentration is per dm³, so the volume must be in dm³: 0.0250 dm³, giving 0.00250 mol.

questions.q: Which procedure produces a solution in which [NaCl] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³? (M(NaCl) = 58.44 g mol⁻¹)
options: Add 0.125 mol of NaCl to 250 cm³ of water and stir until dissolved.
Dissolve 2.92 g of NaCl and make up to 100 cm³ of solution.
Dissolve 0.500 g of NaCl, then make the solution up to 1.00 dm³.
Add 0.500 mol of NaCl to 250 cm³ of water and stir to dissolve it.
optionWhy: A student who divides by the volume of solvent calculates 0.125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.500. Concentration is per volume of solution; dissolving 7.31 g of NaCl increases the volume to about 252 cm³, so [NaCl] ≈ 0.496 mol dm⁻³, not 0.500 mol dm⁻³, and the exact volume is not known. The solution must be made up to a known volume.
[NaCl] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ corresponds to 0.500 × 58.44 = 29.2 g dm⁻³; 100 cm³ of solution therefore needs 2.92 g (0.0500 mol), made up to the mark in a volumetric flask.
A student who reads mol as g puts 0.500 g in each dm³. That is 0.500 ÷ 58.44 = 0.00856 mol, so [NaCl] = 0.00856 mol dm⁻³. The unit mol dm⁻³ means 0.500 mol (29.2 g) per dm³ of solution.

A student who reads [NaCl] as the amount of NaCl uses 0.500 mol, whatever the volume. The solution has a volume of about 260 cm³, so [NaCl] ≈ 1.9 mol dm⁻³; square brackets mean amount per dm³ of solution.
questions.explain: [NaCl] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ corresponds to 0.500 × 58.44 = 29.2 g dm⁻³; 100 cm³ of solution therefore needs 2.92 g (0.0500 mol), made up to the mark in a volumetric flask.
questions.working: Correct procedure: n(NaCl) = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ × 0.100 dm³ = 0.0500 mol; m = nM = 0.0500 mol × 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 2.92 g, made up to 100 cm³ of solution (equivalently, 0.500 mol dm⁻³ = 29.2 g dm⁻³). 0.500 g ÷ 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 0.00856 mol, so 0.500 g in 1.00 dm³ gives 0.00856 mol dm⁻³. 0.500 mol in about 0.260 dm³ of solution gives about 1.9 mol dm⁻³. Adding 0.125 mol to 250 cm³ of water gives a solution whose volume is not 250 cm³, so its concentration is not 0.500 mol dm⁻³ (about 0.496 mol dm⁻³: the solution volume is about 252 cm³).

questions.q: Two identical sealed flasks are at the same temperature and pressure. One is filled with methane, CH₄, and the other with chlorine, Cl₂. The methane flask contains 5.00 × 10²² atoms in total. How many atoms does the chlorine flask contain? (A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01, Cl 35.45)
optionWhy: Equal volumes at the same T and p contain equal numbers of molecules. The CH₄ flask holds 5.00 × 10²² ÷ 5 = 1.00 × 10²² molecules, so the Cl₂ flask also holds 1.00 × 10²² molecules, which contain 2 × 1.00 × 10²² = 2.00 × 10²² atoms.

A student who thinks equal volumes hold equal numbers of atoms gives the same number of atoms as in the CH₄ flask. Avogadro's law counts molecules: each flask holds 1.00 × 10²² molecules, so the Cl₂ flask holds 2.00 × 10²² atoms.

A student who applies the ratio of atoms per molecule the wrong way round calculates 5.00 × 10²² × 5/2 = 1.25 × 10²³. Each Cl₂ molecule has fewer atoms than each CH₄ molecule, so with equal numbers of molecules the Cl₂ flask holds fewer atoms: 5.00 × 10²² × 2/5 = 2.00 × 10²².

A student who thinks equal volumes have equal masses reasons that the Cl₂ flask holds fewer molecules, in the ratio 16.05 : 70.90: 1.00 × 10²² × 16.05 ÷ 70.90 = 2.26 × 10²¹ molecules, or 4.53 × 10²¹ atoms. Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, not equal masses, so the answer is 2.00 × 10²² atoms.
questions.explain: Equal volumes at the same T and p contain equal numbers of molecules. The CH₄ flask holds 5.00 × 10²² ÷ 5 = 1.00 × 10²² molecules, so the Cl₂ flask also holds 1.00 × 10²² molecules, which contain 2 × 1.00 × 10²² = 2.00 × 10²² atoms.
questions.working: By Avogadro's law the flasks contain equal numbers of molecules. N(CH₄ molecules) = 5.00 × 10²² ÷ 5 = 1.00 × 10²² = N(Cl₂ molecules). Each Cl₂ molecule has 2 atoms, so N(atoms) = 2 × 1.00 × 10²² = 2.00 × 10²². (The A_r values are not needed.)

questions.q: Sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 30.0 cm³ of sulfur dioxide? All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
options: 60.0 cm³
30.0 cm³
10.0 cm³
15.0 cm³
optionWhy: A student who uses the mole ratio upside down calculates 30.0 × 2/1 = 60.0 cm³. Only one O₂ is needed for every two SO₂, so V(O₂) = 30.0 × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.
A student who thinks gases react in equal volumes gives 30.0 cm³. The equation's coefficients fix the ratio: 2 volumes of SO₂ react with 1 volume of O₂.

A student who thinks equal volumes hold equal numbers of atoms sets the volumes in the ratio of the atoms in the equation: 2SO₂ contains 6 atoms and O₂ contains 2, so V(O₂) = 30.0 × 2/6 = 10.0 cm³. Avogadro's law counts molecules: the volumes are in the ratio of the coefficients, 2 : 1, so V(O₂) = 30.0 × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.
At the same T and p, gas volumes are in the ratio of the coefficients: V(O₂) = 30.0 cm³ × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.
questions.explain: At the same T and p, gas volumes are in the ratio of the coefficients: V(O₂) = 30.0 cm³ × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.
questions.working: At constant T and p, V ∝ n. From the equation, n(O₂) : n(SO₂) = 1 : 2, so V(O₂) = 30.0 cm³ × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.

questions.q: Which statement is one of the key assumptions of the ideal gas model?
options: The particles lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision.
The spaces between the particles are filled with air that separates them.
The particles repel one another, which keeps them spread through the container.
The particles have a negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas.
optionWhy: A student who thinks moving particles must gradually run down picks this. The model assumes that all collisions are elastic: kinetic energy passes between particles in a collision but the total is not lost, so a gas at constant temperature does not slow down.

A student who cannot accept empty space between particles picks this. In the model the space between the particles is empty. Air is itself a gas made of particles, so it cannot fill the gaps between gas particles.

A student who pictures gas particles pushing each other apart picks this. The model assumes there are no intermolecular forces at all, attractive or repulsive; the gas spreads through the container because its particles move randomly.

This is one of the model's assumptions: the particles are treated as having no volume of their own compared with the space the gas occupies. The other key assumptions are that the particles are moving, exert no intermolecular forces, and collide elastically.
questions.explain: This is one of the model's assumptions: the particles are treated as having no volume of their own compared with the space the gas occupies. The other key assumptions are that the particles are moving, exert no intermolecular forces, and collide elastically.

questions.q: A sample of nitrogen is held at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa, first at 150 K and then at 600 K. It is a gas at both temperatures. At which temperature does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
options: At 150 K, as its particles have stopped moving and so no longer collide
At 150 K, as its slower particles are affected more by the attractions between them
At 600 K, as its faster particles collide more violently with each other
At 600 K, as its particles expand when heated and take up more space
optionWhy: A student who believes particles stop moving when cold picks this. The particles of a gas are always moving: at 150 K nitrogen is still a gas and exerts a pressure because its particles collide with the walls. They move more slowly, which is why the attractions between them matter more.

At low temperature the particles have less kinetic energy, so the intermolecular attractions, which the ideal model ignores, have a significant effect on their motion. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

A student who thinks fast, energetic particles break the model picks this. A real gas behaves more ideally at high temperature, because the particles' kinetic energy is then large compared with the attractions between them. Deviation is greatest at low temperature.

A student who thinks particles swell when heated picks this. Particles do not change size with temperature. At 600 K and the same pressure the gas occupies a larger volume and its particles move faster, so it behaves more ideally, not less.
questions.explain: At low temperature the particles have less kinetic energy, so the intermolecular attractions, which the ideal model ignores, have a significant effect on their motion. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

questions.q: Four gases are each at 300 K and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which gas deviates most from ideal gas behaviour?
options: Helium, He, as its light atoms move the fastest and collide most violently
Neon, Ne, as its atoms are the heaviest and so they occupy the most space
Ammonia, NH₃, as hydrogen bonding attracts its molecules to one another
Methane, CH₄, as each molecule is held together by four C–H bonds
optionWhy: A student who thinks high particle speed makes a gas less ideal picks this. Helium is one of the most nearly ideal gases: its atoms are small and the London forces between them are extremely weak. Fast particles are less affected by attractions, not more.

A student who equates a heavier particle with a larger one, and thinks size decides the deviation, picks this. Neon atoms (M = 20.18 g mol⁻¹) are heavier than ammonia molecules (17.04 g mol⁻¹), but the London forces between them are weak, so neon behaves almost ideally. The strength of the attractions between particles decides the deviation, not their mass.

Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so the attractions between them are much stronger than between the particles of the other three gases. The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces, so the gas with the strongest attractions deviates most.

A student who counts the covalent bonds inside a molecule as the forces between molecules picks this. The four C–H bonds hold each methane molecule together but do not attract one methane molecule to another. Methane molecules attract one another only by London forces, which are much weaker than the hydrogen bonding between ammonia molecules.
questions.explain: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so the attractions between them are much stronger than between the particles of the other three gases. The ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces, so the gas with the strongest attractions deviates most.

questions.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas is kept at constant pressure. Its volume is measured at several temperatures and plotted against temperature in °C. Which description of the graph is correct?
options: A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where volume would be zero
A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where the particles shrink to nothing
A straight line through the origin, since volume is proportional to temperature in °C
A horizontal line, as the gas fills the same container at every temperature
optionWhy: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature. On a Celsius axis the line does not pass through the origin; extended backwards, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), absolute zero. (A real gas would liquefy before this; the line is an extrapolation.)

A student who thinks particles shrink as they cool picks this. The intercept is right but the reason is not: particles do not change size. The volume falls because slower particles hit the walls less hard and less often, so at constant pressure the gas occupies less space.

A student who treats 0 °C as zero temperature picks this. 0 °C is only the melting point of ice, and a gas at 0 °C still has a large volume. Volume is proportional to temperature in kelvin, so on a Celsius axis the line meets the axis at −273 °C.

A student who thinks a gas always has the volume of its container picks this. A gas does fill its container, but at constant pressure the container (for example a gas syringe) expands as the gas is heated, so the volume increases steadily with temperature.
questions.explain: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature. On a Celsius axis the line does not pass through the origin; extended backwards, it reaches zero volume at −273 °C (0 K), absolute zero. (A real gas would liquefy before this; the line is an extrapolation.)

questions.q: What volume is occupied by 0.0472 mol of an ideal gas at 30 °C and 125 kPa? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
optionWhy: A student who leaves the temperature in °C gets 0.0472 × 8.31 × 30 ÷ (1.25 × 10⁵) = 9.41 × 10⁻⁵ m³. PV = nRT needs absolute temperature: 30 °C = 303 K.
A student who substitutes the pressure in kPa gets 0.0472 × 8.31 × 303 ÷ 125 = 0.951 m³, 1000 times too large. With R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ the pressure must be in Pa: 125 kPa = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa.
A student who uses the molar volume at STP gets 0.0472 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 1.07 dm³ = 1.07 × 10⁻³ m³. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ applies only at 273.15 K and 100 kPa; at 303 K and 125 kPa use PV = nRT.

questions.q: A gas syringe contains 2.20 cm³ of an ideal gas at 20 °C and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. What amount of gas does it contain? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
optionWhy: A student who leaves the temperature in °C gets 0.264 ÷ (8.31 × 20) = 1.59 × 10⁻³ mol. PV = nRT needs absolute temperature: 20 °C = 293 K.
A student who converts cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1000, as for dm³, uses V = 2.20 × 10⁻³ m³ and gets 0.108 mol, 1000 times too large. 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 2.20 cm³ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ m³.
A student who uses the molar volume at STP gets 2.20 × 10⁻³ dm³ ÷ 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 9.69 × 10⁻⁵ mol. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ applies only at 273.15 K and 100 kPa; at 293 K and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa use PV = nRT.
